newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Italy's ERM hopes enter critical stage of talks.
newsitem.headline: Italy's ERM hopes enter critical stage of talks.

text.p: Italy's hopes of joining a common European currency enter a high stakes bargaining session on Sunday as EU finance ministers meet to decide a rate of entry for the lira into the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM).

The need to bring together Europe's top policy-makers comes after the EU's monetary committee of central bank and finance ministry officials failed on Saturday to let the lira back into the ERM after a four-year absence.
Rome, officials said, was asking for lira to come in at too weak a level, worrying other European countries that this would give Italy preferential trade terms.
The finance ministers, due to start discussions in the afternoon, will be trying to reach a compromise before Asian markets open in late evening European time, an EU official said.
Another EU official on Sunday played down the significance of Saturday's lack of agreement, saying a ministerial meeting was the most appropriate forum to decide the lira's re-entry.
"The second meeting is fully in line with normal procedures. It isn't at all unprecedented," he said, adding that most major adjustments in the ERM in the past required a top-level meeting.
Italy's failure to win a seat within the ERM could put pressure on the lira and send a strong negative signal over the prospect of a joint European currency.

Re-joining the ERM, from which the lira was unceremoniously dumped amid a currency crisis in 1992, is seen by Italy as crucial to its hopes for being in the first wave of EU countries to adopt the single currency in 1999.
A stable two-year stint within the ERM is one of the qualifying criteria for the new currency, the Euro.

The ERM, a system enhancing monetary stability among member countries, is designed to allow currencies to trade within bands against each other -- for the most part fluctuating by no more than 15 percent from a central rate.
Officials told Reuters that Italy had asked to rejoin at a central rate of 1,010 lira to the German mark, the key currency in the grid.
It was far too weak for the others' blood, however. They said they wanted a rate of less than 1,000 lira to the mark. The lira was trading at about 999 to the mark on Friday.
France has been the most vehement in wanting a stronger rate for the lira, having seen some of its industries battered by a neighbour with a weaker currency.
Italy, like other EU countries which want to join the monetary union from the start, has rushed to meet targets on interest and exchange rates, inflation, the budget deficit and public debt.
Seeking to trim their deficits next year to no more than three percent of gross domestic product, however, some states have unveiled controversial one-off budgetary measures.
Italy has proposed a so-called Euro-tax, a one-off revenue raiser ro help it meet the targets.
If, Italy is brought into the ERM, only three of the EU's 15 countries will be outside the grid.

Britain and Sweden argue that it is not necessary to be in the ERM to qualify for the Euro, it is enough to have a stable rate with the other countries. Both countries are sceptical about the Euro project.
Greece's economy is far weaker that the others and membership of the single currency is all-but ruled out.
